summary: Details the IETF's policies on intellectual property rights, such as patents, relating to technology developed in the IETF. The aim is for working groups to have as much information about IPR constraints as possible. It updates RFC 2026 and, with RFC 3667, replaced its section 10. It has been replaced by RFC 3979.

eli5.summary: If someone owns a patent on a tool, the group should know before using it. This is the rule book saying people must speak up about such claims. RFC 3979 later replaced it.

questions: do ietf participants have to disclose patents
is a patent search required for ietf disclosure
subtitle: The rules for telling the IETF about patents and other rights that may cover a proposed technology.

tldr.problem: As working groups increasingly met claims of patent and other intellectual property rights, the wording of Section 10 of RFC 2026 led to repeated debate over what had to be disclosed, by whom and when.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3668 requires contributors and participants to disclose IPR they reasonably and personally know covers a contribution, sets timing and content rules for disclosures, and has the IETF take no position on validity.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 79) that updates RFC 2026 and RFC 2028, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 3979.

today: RFC 3668 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 3979, so the later document holds the current rules. It updates RFC 2026 and RFC 2028.

sections.title: Why the Rules Were Restated
sections.content:
Since RFC 2026 was published, the exact intent of its Section 10 on IPR disclosures was often debated, because working groups increasingly faced claims of Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) such as patent rights. RFC 3668 clarifies the ambiguities and amplifies the policy. It updates RFC 2026 and, with RFC 3667, replaces Section 10 of RFC 2026. It also updates paragraph 4 of Section 3.2 of RFC 2028.

RFC 2026 set three principles, which this memo keeps: the IETF makes no determination about the validity of any IPR claim; the IETF, following normal processes, may decide to use technology for which IPR disclosures exist; and those contributing must disclose IPR they believe covers or may ultimately cover the technology under discussion. The duty covers IPR of the participant, their employer or sponsor that is reasonably and personally known. No patent search is required.

The memo is not legal advice. A companion, RFC 3667, deals with rights such as copyrights in contributions.
sections.eli5: People argued about what the old rule meant, so this memo explains it again more clearly. The main idea stays: if you know about a claim, say so.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
An IETF Contribution is any submission intended for publication as all or part of an Internet-Draft or RFC, and any statement made within the context of an IETF activity, including oral statements in sessions and messages to working groups, the IESG, the IAB or IETF mailing lists. An RFC Editor Contribution is an Internet-Draft meant for the RFC Editor as an Informational or Experimental RFC, but not as part of the IETF Standards Process.

Reasonably and personally known means something an individual knows personally or would be expected to know because of their job. An organization cannot keep a person in the dark to avoid disclosure, but nobody is required to search for patents.

IPR Covers an Implementing Technology if a valid claim of a patent or application, or other right, would necessarily be infringed by implementing it. Internet-Drafts have a nominal maximum lifetime of 6 months in the Secretariat's public directory.
sections.eli5: The memo first defines its words, such as what counts as handing something in to the group and what it means to know something because of your job.

sections.title: Who Discloses, and When
sections.content:
A contributor who reasonably and personally knows of IPR that they believe covers or may cover their contribution, or that their employer or sponsor may assert against implementations, must disclose it. There are no exceptions. Any other participant who knows of such IPR in someone else's contribution must disclose it too. People who know of IPR they are not required to disclose, for example IPR owned by another company, are encouraged to notify the IETF by email.

Disclosure must be made as soon as reasonably possible after the contribution is published in an Internet-Draft (or RFC, for other participants), unless it is already on file. If the IPR becomes known later, disclosure is due as soon as reasonably possible after that. Participants are strongly encouraged to make at least a preliminary disclosure once a contribution is seriously discussed in a working group.

A person who cannot disclose, for example because an employer forbids it, must not contribute to or take part in IETF activities on that technology. Taking part without making the required disclosure is a violation of IETF process.
sections.eli5: If you know your club's idea uses something you own, you have to say so soon, not wait. If you are not allowed to say, you have to sit that discussion out.

sections.title: What a Disclosure Must Contain
sections.content:
A disclosure must list the numbers of any issued patents or published patent applications, or say the claim rests on unpublished applications. It must name the specific IETF or RFC Editor documents affected, with a version number for an Internet-Draft. Naming the affected sections is helpful when it is not obvious.

A blanket statement of possible IPR on every contribution does not satisfy the requirement, and neither does a blanket promise to license on fair and non-discriminatory terms. A blanket statement of willingness to license all relevant IPR to implementers on a royalty-free basis does satisfy it, as long as any other terms are disclosed.

Licensing information is encouraged but not mandatory. It is helpful to say whether all persons will be able to obtain rights (a) under a royalty-free and otherwise reasonable and non-discriminatory license, (b) under reasonable and non-discriminatory terms that may include a reasonable royalty, or (c) without a license from the IPR holder.
sections.eli5: A good note says exactly what you own and which idea it touches. Saying 'I might own something somewhere' does not count.

sections.title: What the IETF Does With Disclosures
sections.content:
The IESG disclaims any responsibility for identifying or evaluating IPR and takes no position on its validity or scope. Where IPR is disclosed, the IETF Executive Director asks the discloser for a written assurance of licensing under one of the options above. The result does not itself block publication or advancement, though a working group may take it into account and the IESG may defer approval when delay could help obtain assurances. Results are recorded and made available online.

Working groups generally prefer technology with no known IPR claims or with an offer of royalty-free licensing, but they may adopt technology with fair and non-discriminatory terms, or with no licensing commitment, if it is superior enough. For a mandatory-to-implement security technology, IETF consensus is that it should have no known IPR claims or have a royalty-free license available, unless there is a very good reason.

The RFC Editor ensures every IETF RFC carries a standard disclaimer saying the IETF takes no position on the validity or scope of any rights. Specific IPR disclosures must not appear inside IETF documents, since a reader could think the IETF had formed an opinion or that the list was complete.
sections.eli5: The group does not act as a judge of who owns what. It records what people say, prefers free-to-use ideas, and puts a standard warning label in every RFC.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo relates to IETF process, not to any particular technology. It says there are security considerations when adopting any technology, IPR-protected or not, and that a working group should weigh them alongside IPR, but there are no known security issues with the IPR procedures.
sections.eli5: These are rules about paperwork, not about locks, and the memo knows of no safety problem in them.
